headline: Electricity VAT cut takes effect as Burnham's first cost-of-living measure

terms.meaning: Value Added Tax, a tax added to the price of most things you buy
The government's money, held by the Treasury
The government's accounting year, which runs from April to March

levels.headline: Electricity VAT cut takes effect as Burnham's first cost-of-living measure
levels.body:
VAT on household electricity fell from 5% to 0% on Thursday 1 October 2026, the first cost-of-living measure announced by Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The government says the change will save the average household about £45 a year.
Burnham announced the cut at his first cabinet meeting as Prime Minister in July, promising a cost-of-living government, and later confirmed the 1 October start to MPs at Prime Minister's Questions. The zero rate lasts six months, until the end of the financial year in March, and is expected to cost the Exchequer about £850 million in 2026/27.
The cut is funded by cancelling the digital ID programme proposed under Keir Starmer's government, which was meant to become mandatory for right-to-work checks as part of a crackdown on illegal immigration.
The relief covers domestic supplies only. Small businesses that qualify for the domestic rate and are not VAT-registered, charities and residential care homes also benefit.
levels.why: It is the first visible cost-of-living policy of the Burnham government and it replaces a flagship Starmer-era scheme.

levels.headline: Electricity VAT scrapped for six months in Burnham cost-of-living move
levels.body:
VAT on household electricity dropped from 5% to 0% on 1 October, the first cost-of-living policy from Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Ministers say the average household will save around £45 a year.
Burnham announced it at his first cabinet meeting in July and told MPs at Prime Minister's Questions that it would start on 1 October. It runs for six months, to the end of the financial year in March, and will cost the Exchequer roughly £850 million in 2026/27.
The money comes from scrapping the digital ID scheme proposed under Keir Starmer, which would have made ID mandatory for right-to-work checks in the effort to tackle illegal immigration.
Only domestic supplies qualify. Small businesses on the domestic rate that are not VAT-registered, plus charities and residential care homes, also get the benefit.
levels.why: It signals Burnham's priorities and swaps one Starmer policy for a direct help with household bills.

levels.headline: Tax on home electricity cut to zero for six months
levels.body:
The tax on household electricity bills has been cut to zero from today, 1 October. VAT was 5% on domestic electricity. The government says that saves the average home about £45 a year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the plan in July at his first cabinet meeting and promised a government focused on the cost of living. The cut lasts six months, until March, and will cost the Treasury about £850 million this financial year.
To pay for it, the government has cancelled the digital ID programme planned by Keir Starmer's government. That scheme would have required ID for right-to-work checks as part of a crackdown on illegal immigration.
The change applies to homes. Small businesses on the domestic rate that are not registered for VAT, charities and care homes also gain.
levels.why: It should make electricity bills a little cheaper for most households over the winter.

levels.headline: Electricity bills get a tax cut from today
levels.body:
From today, 1 October, there is no VAT on household electricity. The tax used to be 5%. The government says the average household will save around £45 a year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the change in July. He said his government would focus on the cost of living. The cut lasts for six months, until the end of March, and will cost the government around £850 million.
The government is paying for it by dropping the digital ID scheme that Keir Starmer's government had planned. That scheme would have made people prove their right to work using a digital ID, to help stop illegal immigration.
The cut covers homes. Some small businesses, charities and care homes will benefit too, if they pay the domestic rate and are not registered for VAT.
levels.why: It helps with winter bills, but only for six months.

levels.headline: No tax on home electricity for six months, starting today
levels.body:
Today the government stopped charging VAT on electricity used in homes. VAT is a tax added to many things we buy. It was 5% on electricity, and now it is 0%. The government says the typical household will save about £45 a year.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, announced this in July. He wants his government to help with the cost of living, which means the price of everyday things like energy and food. The change will last six months, until the end of March, and it will cost the government about £850 million.
To pay for it, the government has cancelled the digital ID plan made by the last Prime Minister, Keir Starmer. That plan was meant to help check who is allowed to work in the UK.
Small businesses, charities and care homes can benefit too, in some cases.
levels.why: Many families will see slightly lower electricity bills this winter.

levels.headline: Home electricity is cheaper from today because a tax has been removed
levels.body:
From today you do not pay VAT on the electricity you use at home. VAT is a tax that is added to the price of lots of things. On electricity it was 5p for every £1. Now it is nothing. The government thinks a normal home will save about £45 in a year.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said in July that he would do this. He wants to help people with the cost of living, which is how much it costs to pay for things like heating and food. The change lasts for six months, until the end of March.
The government has found the money by cancelling a plan for digital ID cards that the old Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, had started. Those were meant to help check that people have the right to work in the UK.
Some small businesses, charities and care homes will also pay less.
levels.why: It means a small saving on energy bills for lots of families.

levels.headline: The government has taken a tax off home electricity
levels.body:
Today a tax on electricity at home was cut to nothing. The tax is called VAT. People used to pay a bit extra on their electricity bill because of it. Now they do not. A normal family will keep about £45 a year.
The Prime Minister is called Andy Burnham. He took over in July. He said he wanted to help people who find things expensive. When prices go up and money does not stretch as far, we call that the cost of living.
The no-tax rule is for six months, until the end of March. It costs the government a lot of money, about £850 million. To pay for it, the government stopped a plan for digital ID that the last Prime Minister had made. That plan was about checking who can work in the UK.
Some small businesses and charities get cheaper bills too.
levels.why: Families keep a little more of their money while it is cold and dark.

levels.headline: Home electricity is cheaper because the government took off a tax
levels.body:
Today the government stopped a tax on electricity. When you pay for electricity at home, the bill used to include a tax called VAT. Now it does not. A normal family will save about £45 in a year. That is about enough for a few cinema trips.
The new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, promised this in July. He said he wanted to help people with the cost of living. That means how much money people need to pay for things like food and heating.
The change lasts for six months. After that, the government will decide what to do next. It costs the government about £850 million, which is a lot of money. The government is paying for it by stopping a plan for digital ID cards that the last Prime Minister wanted.
Some small shops, charities and care homes pay less as well.
levels.why: A cheaper bill can make a big difference to a family at the start of winter.

levels.headline: Electricity at home now has no tax on it
levels.body:
Today the government made a change. It took a tax off electricity. Electricity is what makes lights and heaters work in your home. A tax is extra money that people must pay to the government. On electricity, the tax was called VAT.
Now there is no VAT on electricity. Bills will be a little smaller. A normal family will keep about £45 each year.
The leader of the country is called the Prime Minister. His name is Andy Burnham. He said he wanted to help families who find things expensive.
The change is only for six months. It stops at the end of March. The government had to find money to pay for it. So it stopped another plan, for digital ID, that the last Prime Minister had made.
Some small shops and care homes will pay less too.
levels.why: A smaller electricity bill helps families to keep warm.

levels.headline: Lights on for less: a tax has been taken off electricity
levels.body:
Imagine you buy a sweet that costs 100p. The shop adds 5p to the price as a tax, so you pay 105p. Today the government said that, for electricity at home, that extra 5p is gone.
The tax is called VAT. The Prime Minister, a man called Andy Burnham, said he would take it off. He wants to help families who find it hard to pay for things. Electricity is what makes lights, the TV and the heating work, so it is something every home needs.
A normal family will save about £45 over a whole year. The change lasts for six months. The government has found the money by stopping a plan for digital ID that the last Prime Minister had started.
Some small shops and care homes also pay less.
levels.why: Families will pay a little less to keep the lights on.

headline: Burnham unveils state-owned Great British Grid at Labour conference

terms.meaning: The network of cables and pylons that carries electricity around the country
Moving a service from public ownership into private companies' hands
Moving electricity over long distances from where it is made to where it is needed

levels.headline: Burnham unveils state-owned Great British Grid at Labour conference
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham used his Labour conference speech on 29 September to announce the Great British Grid, described as the first directly state-owned electricity network since privatisation.
The new publicly owned body will sit as a branch of Great British Energy. Its aims are to cut the time it takes to connect projects to the grid and to bring UK energy costs closer to those in European countries within the next decade.
It will invest in grid infrastructure, with a particular focus on transmission projects and on areas where connection delays are holding back investment. Crucially, it will work alongside the existing network companies rather than replacing them.
The energy industry has broadly welcomed the plan. Industry bodies, analysts and major energy companies have mostly backed the idea of reducing connection bottlenecks, lowering costs and speeding up new grid building, although commentators have questioned whether it will work.
levels.why: It marks a major shift in how Britain's electricity network is owned and could shape energy bills for years.

levels.headline: Great British Grid: first state-owned electricity network since privatisation
levels.body:
Andy Burnham announced the Great British Grid in his Labour conference speech on 29 September. It is described as the first direct state-owned electricity network since privatisation.
It will be a branch of Great British Energy. The goals are shorter waits to connect to the grid and energy costs closer to European levels within a decade.
The body will invest in grid infrastructure, especially transmission projects and places where connection delays are holding back investment. It will work with the existing network companies, not replace them.
Industry bodies, analysts and major energy firms have mostly welcomed it, pointing to the chance of fewer bottlenecks, lower costs and faster building. Some commentators have doubted that it can succeed.
levels.why: It tests whether public ownership can speed up the clean-energy build-out without frightening private investors.

levels.headline: Government to create a publicly owned electricity grid company
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced a new publicly owned company called the Great British Grid. He revealed it in his Labour conference speech on 29 September. It is the first electricity network owned directly by the state since privatisation.
The company will be part of Great British Energy. The government wants it to cut waiting times for new projects to join the grid and to bring energy costs closer to those in European countries within ten years.
It will pay for grid improvements, particularly cables that carry power over long distances and areas where delays are holding back investment. It will work next to the current network companies instead of taking them over.
Most of the energy industry has welcomed the idea, although some commentators have questioned it.
levels.why: Faster grid connections could mean cheaper and cleaner power, but the plan must still prove itself.

levels.headline: Burnham launches state-owned electricity grid company
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has launched the Great British Grid, a new company owned by the state. He announced it in his speech to the Labour conference on 29 September. It is the first state-owned electricity network since the grid was sold off to private firms.
The new company will be part of Great British Energy. The government hopes it will speed up connections to the grid and bring energy costs down towards the level in Europe over the next ten years.
It will invest in the cables and pylons that carry electricity, especially long-distance lines and places where delays are stopping new projects. It will work with the current companies that run the networks, not replace them.
Energy firms and experts have mostly welcomed it. Some commentators are doubtful.
levels.why: The way electricity gets to your home may become cheaper and quicker to improve.

levels.headline: A new state-owned company will help build the electricity grid
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has announced a new company that the government will own. It is called the Great British Grid. The grid is the network of cables and pylons that carries electricity to homes, schools and shops.
In the past, the government sold the grid to private companies. This is the first time since then that the state has owned part of it directly. The new company will be part of Great British Energy.
The aim is to help new power projects join the grid faster, and to bring energy costs closer to those in Europe over the next ten years. The company will work with the firms that already run the network.
Many people in the energy industry say it is a good idea. A few commentators are not sure it will work.
levels.why: If it works, new power projects could start sooner and costs could come down.

levels.headline: The government will own a new part of the electricity network
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has a new plan for electricity. The government will set up a company called the Great British Grid. The grid is the system of cables that brings power to our homes.
Many years ago, the government sold the grid to private firms. This new company is the first part of the network that the government will own directly since then. It will be run as part of another government company, Great British Energy.
The plan is to help new wind farms and power projects join the grid quicker. The government also wants energy to cost less, closer to prices in Europe, within ten years.
The new company will work with the firms that already run the grid. People in the energy industry mostly like the idea. Some commentators have doubts.
levels.why: It could mean new power projects are connected faster and energy costs fall over time.

levels.headline: Burnham plans a new government-owned electricity company
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has announced a new company that the government will own. It is called the Great British Grid. The grid is the system of cables and pylons that carries electricity from power stations and wind farms to homes.
The grid was sold to private firms years ago. This is the first time since then that the state will directly own part of the network. The new company will be a branch of Great British Energy.
The government wants new projects to join the grid more quickly and energy costs to come down towards European levels over ten years. The new company will work with the firms that already run the network.
Most people in the energy industry like the plan, but some commentators doubt it.
levels.why: If it works, it could make electricity cheaper and cleaner over time.

levels.headline: The government will build part of the electricity network itself
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has told people about a new company. It is called the Great British Grid. The government will own it. It will help to build the cables and pylons that carry electricity.
The grid is like a set of roads for electricity. Power stations and wind farms put electricity on the roads, and the roads take it to homes. Years ago, the government sold the roads to private companies. Now it will own some of the new roads itself.
The plan is to stop long waits when new power projects want to join the grid. The government also hopes energy will cost less in ten years.
The new company will work with the old ones. Most energy experts like the idea, but some are not sure.
levels.why: Quicker connections could help bring cheaper, cleaner electricity to everyone.

levels.headline: The government is starting a company for the electricity wires
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has a new plan. The government will start a company called the Great British Grid. It will own some of the cables and pylons that carry electricity.
Electricity is made in power stations and wind farms. The grid carries it to homes. Many years ago, the government sold the grid to private companies. Now it will own a new part of it.
The aim is to stop long waits for new power projects to join. The government hopes energy will cost less in ten years.
The new company will work with the old ones. Most energy experts like the idea. A few are not sure.
levels.why: It could help get cheaper power to homes sooner.

levels.headline: The government is making a new company for electricity roads
levels.body:
Think of electricity as a pizza delivery. The pizza is made in one place and has to travel by road to your home. The grid is the set of roads for electricity. It has cables and big towers called pylons.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says the government will start a new company called the Great British Grid. It will own some of these roads. Long ago the roads were sold to other companies, so this is new.
The plan is to help new power get onto the roads faster, so people do not wait so long. The government also hopes that, in ten years, electricity will cost less.
The new company will work with the old companies. Many people who work with energy think it is a good plan. A few are not sure yet.
levels.why: It is a plan to get electricity to homes faster and, one day, for less money.

headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% but three members want a rise

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences borrowing and saving costs
The Monetary Policy Committee, the nine people who set interest rates
How fast prices are rising

levels.headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% but three members want a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 at its September meeting to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%. Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene again voted for a quarter-point rise to 4%.
The decision comes as higher global energy prices push inflation up. UK CPI inflation rose to 3.1% in August, and the Bank expects it to reach around 3.75% in the final quarter of 2026 and slightly above 4% in early 2027, based on energy prices in mid-September.
Governor Andrew Bailey said higher energy costs had so far had a limited effect on price and wage setting, but warned that the longer the volatility lasted, the bigger the impact on inflation and the more likely a Bank Rate rise would be needed to bring inflation back to the 2% target.
The majority pointed to easing domestic pressures and a soft labour market. UK GDP grew 0.4% in the second quarter, slightly stronger than expected.
levels.why: Borrowing costs for mortgages and loans hinge on this decision, and the Bank is openly warning that a rise could follow.

levels.headline: Bank holds rates at 3.75% with a 6-3 split, warning energy costs may force a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England kept Bank Rate at 3.75% in September, with the Monetary Policy Committee split 6-3. Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene wanted a rise of 0.25 percentage points to 4%.
Higher global energy prices are driving inflation back up. CPI reached 3.1% in August, and the Bank projects around 3.75% in the last quarter of 2026 and just over 4% in early 2027.
Andrew Bailey said the effect on pay and prices had so far been limited, but that the longer volatility lasts, the more likely it is that a rate rise is needed to return inflation to 2%.
The majority judged that weak demand, slack in the jobs market and already tight financial conditions would restrain inflation. GDP rose 0.4% in the second quarter, a little above forecasts.
levels.why: A close vote and a pointed warning suggest the next move could be up, which matters to anyone with a mortgage.

levels.headline: Bank of England leaves interest rates at 3.75% as inflation climbs
levels.body:
The Bank of England has left its main interest rate, Bank Rate, at 3.75%. The committee that sets it voted 6-3. Three members, Huw Pill, Catherine Mann and Megan Greene, wanted a rise to 4%.
Prices are rising faster because of higher world energy costs. Inflation was 3.1% in August and the Bank expects it to reach about 3.75% by the end of the year and just over 4% in early 2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said the effect on prices and wages had been limited so far. But he warned that if the energy price swings carry on, the Bank may have to raise rates to bring inflation back to its 2% target.
Most members felt weak demand and a soft jobs market should hold prices back. The economy grew 0.4% in the second quarter.
levels.why: It affects mortgage and savings rates, and it shows the Bank is leaning towards a possible rise.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay at 3.75%, but a rise could be coming
levels.body:
The Bank of England has decided to keep interest rates at 3.75%. Six of the nine people who vote on this wanted no change. The other three wanted to raise rates to 4%.
The reason for the worry is that energy prices around the world have gone up. That is pushing up prices in the shops and on bills. Inflation, which is how fast prices rise, was 3.1% in August. The Bank thinks it could reach about 3.75% by the end of this year and more than 4% early next year.
The Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey, said the effect on wages and prices had been small so far. But he said that if the problem lasts, rates may need to rise to bring inflation down to the 2% target.
The economy is growing and people are finding jobs harder to get.
levels.why: Anyone with a mortgage or loan should know a rise is possible in the coming months.

levels.headline: The Bank of England keeps interest rates at 3.75% for now
levels.body:
The Bank of England has decided not to change interest rates. They stay at 3.75%. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money. They also decide how much you earn on savings. Six experts voted to keep them the same. Three voted to put them up.
Prices are rising faster at the moment, mostly because energy costs more around the world. In August prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. The Bank thinks that figure could go above 4% early next year. It wants prices to rise by only 2%.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said energy prices had not yet changed pay and prices much. But he said that if they stay high for long, the Bank might need to raise rates.
Most of the experts thought a weak jobs market would help keep prices down.
levels.why: Borrowing could get more expensive if the Bank decides to raise rates.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay the same, but the Bank says they could go up
levels.body:
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. Every few weeks it decides on the interest rate. This rate is the price of borrowing money. If it goes up, loans and mortgages usually cost more. This time the rate stayed at 3.75%. Six people voted for that. Three voted to raise it.
Why might it rise? Prices are going up faster, mainly because energy costs more around the world. Prices were 3.1% higher in August than a year before. The Bank wants that number to be 2%.
The boss of the Bank, Andrew Bailey, said that so far wages and prices have not been pushed up much. But if energy prices stay high, he said, rates may have to go up.
Fewer people are getting new jobs, and the Bank thinks this will help hold prices down.
levels.why: It could change how much people with mortgages or loans pay each month.

levels.headline: The Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% for now
levels.body:
The Bank of England has decided not to change interest rates this time. They stay at 3.75%. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money, and they also set how much you earn on savings. Six people voted to keep the rate the same. Three wanted to raise it to 4%.
Prices are rising faster because energy costs more around the world. Prices in August were 3.1% higher than a year earlier. The Bank thinks the figure could reach about 3.75% by the end of this year and top 4% early next year. It wants only 2%.
The Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey, said energy costs had not yet changed pay and prices much. But he warned rates might have to rise if the problem lasts.
The jobs market is weak, which should help hold prices down.
levels.why: Anyone with a mortgage or a loan could end up paying more if rates rise.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has not changed interest rates yet
levels.body:
There is a bank for the whole country called the Bank of England. It decides how expensive it is to borrow money. That price is called the interest rate. Today it is 3.75%. The Bank has decided to leave it where it is.
Nine people vote on this. Six voted to keep the rate the same. Three said it should go up a little, to 4%.
Why? Things in the shops are getting more expensive, partly because oil and gas cost more all over the world. The Bank wants prices to rise slowly, by only 2% in a year. Right now they are rising faster, by 3.1%.
The boss of the Bank, Andrew Bailey, said that if prices keep going up, the rate may need to rise. That would make borrowing cost more.
levels.why: It affects what families pay on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay the same, but they may go up soon
levels.body:
The Bank of England has kept interest rates at 3.75%. Interest rates are the price of borrowing money. If they go up, loans and mortgages usually cost more. Six people voted to leave the rate where it is. Three voted to put it up.
Prices are going up faster now. In August they were 3.1% higher than a year before. The Bank wants prices to rise by only 2%. Energy costs more around the world, and that is pushing prices up.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said that if energy stays dear, rates may have to go up. That would make borrowing cost more.
Fewer jobs are being offered, which should help hold prices down.
levels.why: It could change how much families pay on mortgages and loans.

levels.headline: The people who set interest rates have decided to wait
levels.body:
Imagine a school tuck shop that lets you borrow pocket money. You pay a little extra when you give it back. That extra is like an interest rate. A big bank for the whole country, the Bank of England, sets the rate for the whole country.
The Bank has said the extra will stay the same for now. Six of the nine people voted to wait. Three wanted to make it a little bigger.
Why would they want that? Sweets, bills and food are getting more expensive. The Bank wants prices to go up slowly. If prices rise too fast, it can make the extra bigger to slow things down.
The boss, Andrew Bailey, said it might have to do that if energy keeps costing a lot.
levels.why: The Bank is making sure prices do not rise too quickly for families.

headline: UK economy grew 0.5% in the second quarter, revised up from 0.4%

terms.meaning: Gross domestic product, the total value of everything the economy produces
A group of seven large rich economies, including the UK, US, Germany, France, Japan, Italy and Canada
Parts of the economy that sell things other than goods, such as shops, banks and restaurants

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.5% in the second quarter, revised up from 0.4%
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.5% between April and June 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics, revised up from an initial estimate of 0.4%. The figure was published on 30 September.
GDP in the second quarter was 1.4% higher than a year earlier, up from an initial estimate of 1.2%. Growth in the first quarter was 0.6%, so the first half of the year was stronger than previously thought and places the UK near the top of the G7 group of rich economies.
The upward revision came largely from services, which grew more strongly than first estimated, and the figures also showed household income and business investment rising. That means the economy is slightly larger than earlier calculations suggested.
The stronger picture sits alongside rising inflation and warnings from the Bank of England about energy prices, which could slow growth later in the year.
levels.why: It shows the economy entered the autumn in better shape than expected, even as energy costs push prices up.

levels.headline: UK growth revised up to 0.5% for April to June
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics said on 30 September that UK GDP grew 0.5% in the second quarter of 2026, up from a first estimate of 0.4%.
On an annual basis, output was 1.4% higher than a year earlier, revised from 1.2%. With 0.6% growth in the first quarter, the first half of the year leads or comes near the top of the G7.
Services growth was stronger than previously estimated, and household income and business investment both rose. The economy is therefore a little larger than earlier figures showed.
The better data arrives at an awkward time: inflation is rising on higher energy costs, and the Bank of England has warned that further rises in Bank Rate may be needed if the volatility continues.
levels.why: Strong growth gives the government more room, but rising prices could soon cut into it.

levels.headline: UK economy grew faster than first thought this summer
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.5% between April and June, the Office for National Statistics has said. Its first estimate was 0.4%. The new figure came out on 30 September.
Compared with a year earlier, the economy was 1.4% bigger, not the 1.2% first reported. The economy also grew 0.6% in the first three months of the year. That puts the UK near the top of the G7 group of big rich countries for the first half of 2026.
Most of the upgrade came from services, such as shops, banks and restaurants. Household income and business investment also rose.
But prices are rising faster because of higher energy costs, and the Bank of England has said it may have to raise interest rates.
levels.why: It suggests households and firms are doing better than feared, though rising prices are a worry.

levels.headline: UK economy grew a little faster than first reported
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.5% between April and June this year. The first estimate was 0.4%. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, shared the new figure on 30 September.
The economy is now 1.4% bigger than it was a year ago. The first guess was 1.2%. It also grew 0.6% in the first three months of the year. Over the first half of 2026, the UK did better than most of the other big rich countries in the G7.
Much of the improvement came from services, such as shops, restaurants and banks. People's incomes and the money businesses spend on new equipment went up as well.
The good news comes while prices are rising and the Bank of England is thinking about raising interest rates.
levels.why: Growth usually helps with jobs and wages, but higher prices could still squeeze budgets.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew more than first thought
levels.body:
The UK economy is the total of everything people and businesses make and sell. The experts who count it say it grew by 0.5% between April and June. At first they thought it was 0.4%.
Compared with a year ago, the economy is 1.4% bigger. The experts first said 1.2%. Over the first six months of 2026, the UK grew faster than most of the other big, rich countries in a group called the G7.
Most of the extra growth came from services. Services are things like restaurants, banks and shops. Families also had more money coming in, and businesses spent more on things they need.
But prices are going up faster now, because energy costs more. That could hold the economy back later.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and better pay, though rising prices still matter.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a bit more than experts first said
levels.body:
Every few months, experts count how much the whole country made and sold. This is how they measure the economy. For April to June, they said it grew by 0.5%. First they thought it grew by 0.4%.
The economy is also 1.4% bigger than a year ago. In the first half of the year, the UK did better than most big rich countries.
Most of the growth came from services, which means things like shops, banks and cafes. Families also had a bit more money, and companies spent more on new things.
But there is a worry. Energy costs more now, so prices are rising faster. The Bank of England has said it might raise interest rates, which makes borrowing cost more.
levels.why: Growth is good for jobs, but families will still feel higher prices.

levels.headline: UK economy grew a little more than experts first said
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.5% between April and June this year, according to the Office for National Statistics. The first guess had been 0.4%. The new figure was shared on 30 September.
The economy is now 1.4% bigger than it was a year ago. The first guess was 1.2%. In the first three months of the year it grew 0.6%, so the UK did better than most of the big rich countries in the G7 over the first half of the year.
Most of the extra growth came from services, such as shops, restaurants and banks. People's incomes and business spending also rose.
But prices are rising faster because energy costs more, and that could hold the economy back.
levels.why: Growth can help create jobs and raise pay, even if prices are a worry.

levels.headline: The UK made and sold more than experts first thought
levels.body:
Experts count how much a country makes and sells. They call this the economy. When it gets bigger, we say it has grown. Between April and June, the UK economy grew by 0.5%. The experts first said 0.4%, so it was a nicer surprise.
A year ago, the economy was smaller. It is now 1.4% bigger than then. It also grew in the first three months of the year. So far this year, the UK has done better than most big, rich countries.
Most of the growth came from things like shops, banks and cafes. Families had a bit more money, and companies spent more.
But things are getting more expensive because energy costs more. So the good news may not last all year.
levels.why: It is a sign the economy is holding up, even though prices are climbing.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew more than experts first thought
levels.body:
The economy is everything a country makes and sells. Experts say the UK economy grew by 0.5% between April and June. They first thought 0.4%. They told us on 30 September.
Compared with a year ago, it is 1.4% bigger. In the first half of the year, the UK did better than most other big rich countries.
Most of the growth came from services. Services means things like cafes, shops and banks. Families also had a bit more money, and businesses spent more.
But things are getting dearer because energy costs more. The Bank of England may raise interest rates, which makes borrowing cost more.
levels.why: A growing economy is good for jobs, but dearer prices still matter.

levels.headline: The country made and sold a bit more than before
levels.body:
Think of the whole country as one huge school fair. Everyone makes things, like cakes and crafts, and sells them. If more is made and sold than before, the fair has grown. The country's grown-ups who count this say the fair grew by a small amount from April to June.
First they thought it grew by 0.4. Now they say 0.5. That is a tiny bit more. Over the whole year it grew by 1.4. That is better than most big, rich countries.
Shops, banks and cafes sold more than before. Families also had a little more money to spend.
But things are getting more expensive, because gas and oil cost more. That can make the fair harder to run later.
levels.why: A bigger economy is usually good news for jobs and pay.

headline: FTSE 100 slips and 10-year gilt yield stays near 19-year high at 5.41%

terms.meaning: A bond issued by the UK government, which is a way of lending it money
The return an investor gets on a bond, which rises when the bond's price falls
An index of the 100 biggest companies listed on the London Stock Exchange

levels.headline: FTSE 100 slips and 10-year gilt yield stays near 19-year high at 5.41%
levels.body:
The FTSE 100 closed at 10,606.00 on Wednesday 30 September, down 30.71 points, or 0.29%, from the previous day's close of 10,636.71. The index hit 10,725 in the opening minutes but faded through the day.
Traders pointed to hot inflation data in Europe and elevated global bond yields, which outweighed softer US inflation figures and steadier oil prices. Sterling fell 0.43% to $1.3206.
The yield on the UK 10-year gilt closed at 5.41%, close to levels last seen about 19 years ago. A gilt yield is the return investors demand for lending to the government. It rises when investors sell bonds, and it feeds through into the cost of mortgages and government borrowing.
Markets are worried about persistent inflation and a more hawkish Bank of England, which has said it may raise rates.
levels.why: High gilt yields raise the government's borrowing costs and tend to push up mortgage rates.

levels.headline: London shares dip as 10-year gilt yield holds at 5.41%
levels.body:
The FTSE 100 ended Wednesday 30 September at 10,606.00, down 0.29% on the day. It reached 10,725 early on before sliding.
Strong European inflation data and high global bond yields weighed more than softer US inflation and stable oil prices. Sterling dropped 0.43% to $1.3206.
The 10-year gilt yield closed at 5.41%, near 19-year highs, as investors worry about persistent inflation and a Bank of England that is leaning towards higher rates.
Higher gilt yields mean it costs the government more to borrow and can feed into mortgage and loan pricing. The Bank of England kept Bank Rate at 3.75% this month but three members voted for a rise.
levels.why: The bond market is sending a warning about borrowing costs for both the Treasury and households.

levels.headline: UK shares fall slightly while the cost of government borrowing stays high
levels.body:
The FTSE 100, the index of London's biggest listed companies, closed at 10,606 on Wednesday, down 0.29%. It had climbed early in the day but lost its gains.
Investors were unsettled by high inflation figures in Europe and by high bond yields around the world. The pound also fell by 0.43% against the US dollar to $1.3206.
The yield on the UK's 10-year government bond, called a gilt, closed at 5.41%. That is near its highest for about 19 years. The yield is the interest investors demand to lend to the government.
Persistent inflation and a Bank of England that may raise rates are keeping yields high. That makes it more expensive for the government to borrow.
levels.why: It affects how much the government pays to borrow, and may affect mortgage costs.

levels.headline: London shares dip as the cost of government borrowing stays high
levels.body:
The FTSE 100 is a list of the 100 biggest companies on the London stock market. It ended Wednesday at 10,606, which is 0.29% lower than the day before. It had risen early on but gave up the gains.
Investors were worried by high inflation in Europe and by high interest on bonds around the world. The pound also fell a little, by 0.43%, to $1.3206.
The UK government borrows by selling bonds called gilts. The 10-year gilt now pays investors 5.41% a year, which is close to the highest level for about 19 years.
That figure stays high because inflation is a worry and the Bank of England may raise interest rates. It means the government pays more to borrow, and mortgage lenders often follow.
levels.why: If the government has to pay more to borrow, that can affect taxes, spending and mortgages.

levels.headline: The cost of the government borrowing money stays high
levels.body:
The government borrows money by selling bonds. In the UK, these bonds are called gilts. Buyers want interest for lending. On Wednesday, the interest on the 10-year gilt was 5.41% a year. That is almost the highest for about 19 years.
Why is it so high? People are worried that prices will keep rising. Prices went up faster in Europe, and the Bank of England may put interest rates up. When investors expect higher rates, they ask for more interest.
On the stock market, the FTSE 100, which lists the 100 biggest companies in London, fell a little to 10,606. The pound also lost a little against the dollar.
When the government pays more to borrow, it has less to spend on other things. Mortgage prices often follow gilt costs.
levels.why: It matters for taxes, spending and how much families pay on mortgages.

levels.headline: The government is paying a lot of interest to borrow money
levels.body:
Sometimes the government needs more money than it has. So it borrows, by selling bonds. In the UK they are called gilts. People who buy them are lending money, and they get interest back. The interest rate on the 10-year gilt is now 5.41%. That is almost as high as it has been for 19 years.
Why so high? People are worried that prices will keep rising. Prices rose fast in Europe. The Bank of England may also raise interest rates. So the people lending want more interest.
On Wednesday the FTSE 100 also fell a bit. That is a list of the 100 biggest companies in London. The pound lost a bit of value against the dollar too.
When the government pays more interest, there is less left to spend on schools and hospitals.
levels.why: It can mean less money for public services, and dearer mortgages.

levels.headline: Government borrowing costs stay high while London shares dip
levels.body:
The government borrows money by selling bonds called gilts. People who buy them are lending money, and they get interest. On Wednesday the interest on the 10-year gilt was 5.41% a year, close to the highest in about 19 years.
It is high because people are worried that prices will keep rising, and the Bank of England may raise interest rates. Inflation also rose faster in Europe.

When the government pays more interest, it has less money to spend on other things. Mortgage lenders often follow gilt costs, so homes can get dearer to finance.
levels.why: It affects taxes, public spending and the cost of mortgages.

levels.headline: The government's borrowing is getting expensive
levels.body:
If you borrow money, you usually have to pay back a bit extra. The extra is called interest. The government borrows money too. It does this by selling something called a gilt. The person who buys it is lending money, and they are paid interest.
Right now, the interest on the 10-year gilt is 5.41% a year. That is almost the highest in about 19 years. It is high because people are worried that prices will keep going up, and that the Bank of England may make borrowing dearer.
On Wednesday the stock market in London also dipped a bit. It is a list of the 100 biggest firms. The pound lost a little value against the dollar as well.
If borrowing is dear for the government, there is less left for other things.
levels.why: It could mean less money for things like schools, and higher costs for homeowners.

levels.headline: The government is paying a lot of interest to borrow money
levels.body:
When the government needs money, it borrows. It sells bonds called gilts. The people who buy them get interest. Now the interest on the 10-year gilt is 5.41% a year. That is almost the highest for 19 years.
It is high because people worry that prices will keep going up. The Bank of England might also raise interest rates.
On Wednesday, the London stock market also fell a little. The stock market is where people buy and sell parts of big companies. The pound lost a bit of value against the dollar.
When the government pays more interest, it has less to spend on schools and hospitals. Mortgages can get dearer too.
levels.why: Less money for services, and dearer mortgages, can follow.

levels.headline: The government has to pay a lot to borrow money
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow £10 from your friend. Your friend says you must give back £10 and a bit extra. That extra is called interest. The government also borrows money. People who lend it money get interest back.
Right now the government is paying about 5p extra for every £1, each year, on a loan that lasts ten years. That is nearly the most it has had to pay for 19 years. It is a lot because people worry that prices will keep going up.
On Wednesday, the shares of big firms in London dipped a tiny bit too. The pound also lost a bit of value against the dollar.
When the government pays more extra, it has less money left for things like schools and parks.
levels.why: It is like having less pocket money left after paying someone back.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% in August as petrol and diesel push prices up

terms.meaning: Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of how fast prices are rising
Inflation leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, which can swing a lot
A measure of inflation that also includes housing costs for people who own their homes

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% in August as petrol and diesel push prices up
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, the Office for National Statistics said on 16 September. The largest upward contributions came from petrol and diesel prices.
The broader CPIH measure, which includes housing costs for owner-occupiers, rose to 3.3% from 3.1%. Core CPI, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was unchanged at 2.6%.
On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.5% in August, compared with a rise of 0.3% in August last year.
The jump reflects higher global energy prices and has shaped the Bank of England's thinking. It left Bank Rate at 3.75% this month but said inflation could reach around 3.75% in the final quarter of 2026. The next inflation figures are due on 21 October.
levels.why: Rising fuel costs are pulling the headline rate away from the Bank's 2% target and feeding into interest-rate decisions.

levels.headline: CPI inflation climbs to 3.1% as fuel costs bite
levels.body:
Annual CPI inflation was 3.1% in August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, the ONS reported on 16 September. Petrol and diesel prices made the largest upward contributions.
CPIH, which includes owner-occupiers' housing costs, rose to 3.3% from 3.1%. Core CPI was steady at 2.6%.
Monthly CPI rose 0.5%, against a 0.3% rise in August 2025.
The pick-up is driven by global energy prices, which is why the Bank of England expects inflation of around 3.75% in the fourth quarter. The steady core rate suggests underlying domestic price pressure has not yet worsened. The next release is on 21 October.
levels.why: The pattern of rising headline and steady core inflation is central to the Bank's rate decisions.

levels.headline: Prices rose 3.1% in the year to August, driven by fuel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.1% higher in August than a year earlier, up from 2.9% in July, the Office for National Statistics said on 16 September. The biggest push came from higher petrol and diesel prices.
A wider measure that includes housing costs for homeowners, called CPIH, rose to 3.3% from 3.1%. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was steady at 2.6%.
Over the month of August alone, prices rose 0.5%. A year earlier the monthly rise was 0.3%.
The rise is linked to higher energy prices around the world. The Bank of England has said it expects inflation to reach about 3.75% by the end of the year. The next figures come out on 21 October.
levels.why: Higher prices reduce what wages can buy, and they influence interest rates.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.1% because petrol and diesel cost more
levels.body:
Prices in the shops and on the forecourt were 3.1% higher in August than a year before. The month before, the figure was 2.9%. The Office for National Statistics shared this on 16 September. Petrol and diesel were the biggest reason for the rise.
A wider measure of inflation that also counts housing costs for people who own their homes was 3.3%. Core inflation, which leaves out things that jump around, like energy and food, stayed at 2.6%.
In August alone, prices rose by 0.5%. Last year the rise in the same month was 0.3%.
Energy costs more around the world, and that is pushing prices up. The next set of figures comes out on 21 October.
levels.why: Money does not go as far as it did, and the Bank of England is watching closely.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, with petrol and diesel the main cause
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In August, prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. In July, the figure was 2.9%. The experts who count prices shared the new number on 16 September.
The biggest reason was the cost of petrol and diesel. Another figure, which includes housing costs for people who own their homes, was 3.3%. A third figure, which leaves out food, energy, alcohol and tobacco because they jump around a lot, stayed at 2.6%.
There is a target for inflation. The Bank of England wants it to be 2%. Now it is above that.
The next figures come out on 21 October. Energy costs more around the world, so prices may keep rising.
levels.why: Things cost more, so wages and pocket money do not go as far.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, mostly because fuel costs more
levels.body:
Prices go up a bit every year. We call that inflation. In August, things cost 3.1% more than a year before. In July, it was 2.9%. So prices are rising a bit faster now. The experts who count prices told us on 16 September.
The biggest reason was petrol and diesel. They cost more than they did. Experts also look at another number that leaves out food and energy, because those jump around a lot. That number did not change. It stayed at 2.6%.
The Bank of England wants prices to go up by only 2% in a year. So 3.1% is a bit too high.
The next price figures come out on 21 October.
levels.why: It means your money buys a little less than it used to.

levels.headline: Prices rise 3.1% in the year to August because fuel costs more
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.1% higher in August than a year before. In July the figure was 2.9%. The experts who count prices shared this on 16 September. Petrol and diesel were the main reason.
Another figure also counts housing costs for people who own their homes. It rose to 3.3%. A third figure leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, because they jump around a lot. That one stayed at 2.6%.
In August alone, prices rose by 0.5%. A year earlier, the rise in the same month was 0.3%.
The Bank of England wants prices to rise by only 2% a year, so 3.1% is too high. The next figures come out on 21 October.
levels.why: It means wages and pocket money buy a little less.

levels.headline: Things cost more because petrol and diesel got dearer
levels.body:
When things cost more than they did last year, we call that inflation. Last month, the experts who count prices said that things cost 3.1% more than a year ago. For every £100 you spent last year, you now spend £103.10 to buy the same things.
The biggest reason was petrol and diesel, the fuel that powers cars and vans. They cost more. Oil is dearer around the world.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It wants prices to rise by only 2%, so 3.1% is a bit high. If prices rise too fast, it can make borrowing cost more to slow things down.
The next numbers come out on 21 October.
levels.why: Families have to spend more to buy the same things.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster because petrol and diesel cost more
levels.body:
Inflation is how fast prices go up. In August, things cost 3.1% more than a year before. In July it was 2.9%. The experts who count prices told us on 16 September.
Petrol and diesel were the biggest reason. They cost more, because oil is dearer around the world.
Experts also look at a number that leaves out food and energy, because they jump around. That number stayed at 2.6%.
The Bank of England wants prices to go up by only 2% a year. So 3.1% is too high. If prices keep rising, the Bank may make borrowing cost more.
The next numbers come out on 21 October.
levels.why: Things cost more, so money does not go as far.

levels.headline: Prices are creeping up because fuel costs more
levels.body:
Imagine your favourite snack cost £1 last year. This year it costs a few pence more. If most things cost a few pence more, we call that inflation. This time, prices are 3 pence higher for every £1, a little more than last month.
The biggest reason is petrol and diesel. They are fuels that make cars and lorries go. They cost more now, so lots of other things cost more too.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It would like prices to go up by only 2 pence for every £1. So it is watching closely.
The experts will count prices again on 21 October.
levels.why: Your pocket money would buy a tiny bit less this year.

headline: Conservatives gather in Birmingham for conference as Badenoch targets Burnham

levels.headline: Conservatives gather in Birmingham for conference as Badenoch targets Burnham
levels.body:
The Conservative Party conference opens on Sunday 4 October at the Birmingham ICC and the Hyatt Regency Hotel, and runs until Wednesday 7 October 2026.
It is the first Tory conference since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July. Kemi Badenoch, who has led the party and served as Leader of the Opposition since 2 November 2024, has said the Conservatives will turn the tide on what she calls Burnham's destructive socialist agenda.
The conference follows Labour's gathering in Liverpool, where Burnham announced the Great British Grid and other reforms, and comes as Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage, has grown into a major force among voters worried about immigration and the economy.
Badenoch will be expected to set out how the Conservatives plan to win back voters, and the government's recent measures, such as the electricity VAT cut, will form part of the debate.
levels.why: The conference is a key chance for the Conservatives to show voters they can recover from their election defeat.

levels.headline: Tories head to Birmingham with Badenoch under pressure to set out a path back

headline: Iran says it has received US reply to its Hormuz proposal as mediated talks continue

terms.meaning: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped
When ships are stopped from entering or leaving ports
Penalties, usually trade restrictions, placed on a country

levels.headline: Iran says it has received US reply to its Hormuz proposal as mediated talks continue
levels.body:
Iran confirmed on 30 September that it had received Washington's response to its seven-day proposal on the Strait of Hormuz, passed on through Qatari mediators. A government spokeswoman did not say what the response contained.
Qatari officials met Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Doha on 29 September after returning from Washington, and he was expected to review the reply with officials in Tehran on 30 September. The US and Iran have also held separate mediator talks, including in New York.
Iran's proposal calls for the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions on Iranian oil and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports within four to five days, with nuclear talks starting within seven days. Tehran has tied any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to those steps.
The conflict began in February, and the standoff has disrupted oil shipments from the Gulf.
levels.why: Whether the Strait of Hormuz reopens affects oil prices and living costs far beyond the Middle East.

levels.headline: US-Iran diplomacy continues through Qatar over Hormuz reopening
levels.body:
Iran said on 30 September that it had received the US response to its seven-day Hormuz proposal via Qatari mediators. Its spokeswoman did not reveal the content.
Qatari officials met Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Doha on 29 September, and he was due to review the reply in Tehran. The two sides have held separate mediator talks, including in New York.
Tehran wants the US to release frozen funds, lift sanctions on Iranian oil and end the naval blockade of its ports within four to five days, with nuclear talks beginning within seven days. It has tied any reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to those steps.
The war, which began in February, has disrupted Gulf oil exports.
levels.why: A deal could ease pressure on global energy prices, while a breakdown would keep them high.

levels.headline: Iran gets US answer on plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
Iran says it has received the United States' reply to its proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The message was passed on by mediators from Qatar. Iran's government spokeswoman did not say what the reply said.
The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, met Qatari officials in Doha on 29 September and was expected to discuss the reply in Tehran. The US and Iran have also held separate talks through mediators.
Iran wants the US to release frozen Iranian money, lift sanctions on its oil and end the blockade of its ports by the US navy within about five days. It also wants nuclear talks to begin within a week. Iran says the Strait will only reopen once those things happen.
The war began in February.
levels.why: The strait carries a big share of the world's oil, so the talks matter to prices everywhere.

levels.headline: Iran has the US answer to its plan to reopen a key sea route
levels.body:
Iran says the United States has replied to its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. This is a narrow sea route that lots of the world's oil ships pass through. The reply came through mediators from Qatar. Iran has not said what the reply says.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, met Qatari officials on 29 September. He was due to look at the reply with officials in Tehran. The two countries have also had separate talks through mediators.
Iran wants the US to free its frozen money, remove limits on selling its oil, and stop blocking its ports, all within about five days. It also wants talks about its nuclear programme to start within a week. Iran says it will only reopen the route after that.
The war began in February.
levels.why: Oil moves through this sea route, so what happens affects petrol prices.

levels.headline: Iran and the US are still talking about a key sea route
levels.body:
Iran and the United States are fighting a war that began in February. Now they are also talking, through helpers from a country called Qatar. These helpers are called mediators.
The talks are about the Strait of Hormuz. It is a narrow stretch of sea. Lots of the world's oil ships go through it. At the moment its traffic is disrupted. Iran sent a plan to reopen it. On 30 September it said it had a reply from the US, but it did not say what was in it.
Iran wants the US to give back its frozen money, let it sell oil, and stop blocking its ports. It also wants talks on nuclear weapons to start quickly. Iran says it will reopen the strait only if those things happen.
levels.why: If the sea route opens, oil should get cheaper for people everywhere.

levels.why: Oil travels through this sea route, so it affects what we pay for fuel.

The war began in February.
levels.why: Oil moves through this route, so the talks affect petrol prices.

headline: Brent crude falls to about $97 as Gulf exports recover and US-Iran talks continue

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for a barrel of oil

levels.headline: Brent crude falls to about $97 as Gulf exports recover and US-Iran talks continue
levels.body:
Brent crude futures fell 1.1% to $96.92 a barrel on 1 October, extending a retreat from earlier in the week. On Tuesday, Brent had closed down 2.6% at $102.59.
Two things are easing supply fears. Crude exports from Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports have recovered after an attack on a key pipeline earlier this month, and US crude inventories unexpectedly rose. Gulf crude exports reached 12.8 million barrels a day in September, the highest since the war began, though still well below the 18.8 million barrels a day in February.
Investors are also watching renewed US-Iran diplomacy over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Despite the fall, Brent recorded a gain of around 14% in September, its biggest monthly rise since July, so prices remain high and are feeding into petrol costs and inflation.
levels.why: Oil is the main reason UK inflation is rising, so its direction matters for fuel bills and interest rates.

levels.headline: Brent slips below $100 as Saudi exports recover and diplomacy continues

levels.why: Falling oil would ease pressure on prices, but the gains this month show how fragile the picture is.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall as Gulf exports recover

The price of Brent crude, the main international benchmark for oil, fell 1.1% to $96.92 a barrel on 1 October. On Tuesday it had closed 2.6% lower at $102.59.
Prices are falling because supply fears are easing. Saudi Arabia's exports from its Red Sea ports have recovered after an attack on an important pipeline earlier this month. US oil stocks also rose unexpectedly. Gulf oil exports reached 12.8 million barrels a day in September, the highest since the war began, though still below the 18.8 million in February.
Traders are also watching talks between the US and Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Even so, Brent rose about 14% in September, its biggest monthly rise since July.
levels.why: Oil prices feed directly into petrol prices and the cost of living.

levels.headline: Oil gets a little cheaper as supplies return
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the main world price for oil, fell to $96.92 a barrel on 1 October. That was 1.1% lower than the day before. On Tuesday it ended at $102.59.
The price is dropping because people are less worried about running short. Saudi Arabia is sending oil from its Red Sea ports again after an attack on a key pipeline earlier this month. America also has more oil in store than expected. In September, the Gulf region exported 12.8 million barrels a day, the most since the war began. In February, it was 18.8 million.
Traders are also watching talks between the US and Iran.
But over September as a whole, oil rose about 14%.
levels.why: Cheaper oil would help to bring down petrol prices.

levels.headline: Oil prices fall because more supplies are arriving

People are also watching talks between the US and Iran.
Over the whole of September, oil still went up about 14%.
levels.why: Oil prices affect the cost of petrol, heating and many other things.

headline: Russia pounds Kyiv power grid in first mass assault since last autumn

terms.meaning: The network that carries electricity from power stations to homes and businesses
A military alliance of countries including the UK, US and most of Europe
An alarm that warns people to take shelter from attack

levels.headline: Russia pounds Kyiv power grid in first mass assault since last autumn
levels.body:
Russia launched a day-long missile and drone assault on Ukraine on 30 September, targeting the power grid in what was reported as its first mass attack on Kyiv since last autumn. Four people were killed and eight injured in the Kyiv region.
Air raid sirens sounded over the capital for more than 20 hours, one of the longest sustained attacks it has faced since the full-scale invasion began. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said seven people were killed across the country, including a child.
NATO aircraft were scrambled in Poland and Romania overnight into Wednesday morning as the barrage unfolded.
The attack on energy infrastructure comes as winter approaches, when Ukraine's need for heat and light rises sharply, and underlines the pressure on Ukraine's allies, including the UK, to keep supporting its air defences.
levels.why: Attacks on power stations are meant to leave Ukrainians without heat and light in winter, and they test Western support.

levels.headline: Russian barrage hits Kyiv grid, killing four in region
levels.body:

levels.why: The strikes raise the stakes for winter and for Western air-defence supplies.

levels.headline: Russia attacks Ukraine's power grid in one of the longest assaults on Kyiv

Russia attacked Ukraine with missiles and drones throughout 30 September, aiming mainly at the power grid. It was the first mass assault on Kyiv since last autumn, reports said. Four people were killed and eight hurt in the Kyiv region.

Winter is coming, and attacks on power stations can leave people without heating and light. Ukraine's allies, including the UK, are being urged to supply more air defences.
levels.why: Without electricity in winter, ordinary Ukrainians face real hardship.

levels.why: It means a harder winter for Ukrainians, and more calls for help from other countries.

Planes from NATO, a group of friendly countries, flew up in Poland and Romania.
Winter is coming. Without electricity, homes are cold and dark.

headline: Fed raises rates to 3.75%-4% in its first increase since 2023

terms.meaning: The US central bank's main interest rate
One hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 basis points is a quarter of a percentage point
The Federal Reserve's preferred measure of US inflation

levels.headline: Fed raises rates to 3.75%-4% in its first increase since 2023
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark federal funds rate by 25 basis points on 16 September, to a target range of 3.75% to 4%. It was the first increase since 2023, and the decision of the policy committee was unanimous, 12-0.
The meeting was led by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who said inflation was still too high. Markets now expect at least one more quarter-point rise in 2026, and a further series of increases into 2027.
The latest US data offers some relief. Inflation figures released on 30 September came in below expectations, but other data suggested the economy was stronger in the spring than first thought, which helped keep bond yields high.
The S&P 500 fell 0.25% to 7,651.54 that day and lost 0.5% over September, while the Dow dropped 4.3% and the Nasdaq rose 1.9%.
levels.why: What the Fed does steers borrowing costs across the world, including in the UK.

levels.headline: Fed hikes rates for the first time since 2023 as Warsh says inflation is too high
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve lifted its federal funds rate by a quarter of a point to 3.75%-4% on 16 September. The committee voted 12-0, and it was the first rise since 2023.
Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation was still too high. Markets now price in at least one more rise this year and further increases into 2027.
Data on 30 September showed US inflation slowing by more than expected, but reports suggesting the economy had been stronger in the spring than thought kept bond yields high and weighed on shares. The S&P 500 closed down 0.25% at 7,651.54, finishing September 0.5% lower. The Dow lost 4.3% in the month, while the Nasdaq gained 1.9%.
levels.why: Higher US rates tend to lift global yields and strengthen the dollar, which affects UK borrowing too.

levels.headline: US central bank raises interest rates for the first time in three years
levels.body:
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point on 16 September. The rate is now between 3.75% and 4%. It is the first rise since 2023, and all 12 members of the committee voted for it.
The Fed's new chair, Kevin Warsh, said inflation was still too high. Investors expect at least one more rise this year, and more in 2027.
On 30 September, new figures showed US inflation was lower than expected, but the economy also looked stronger than thought earlier in the year. That kept the interest on government bonds high. The S&P 500 share index fell 0.25% that day and ended September 0.5% down.
levels.why: Rates in the US influence the cost of borrowing around the world.

levels.headline: The US raises interest rates for the first time since 2023
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. On 16 September it put up its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to between 3.75% and 4%. This is the first rise since 2023. All 12 people who voted were in favour.
The Fed's new boss, Kevin Warsh, said that prices are still rising too fast. Investors think there will be at least one more rise this year, and more next year.
On 30 September, new figures showed prices rising more slowly than experts had expected. But the US economy also looked stronger than thought, so rates on government bonds stayed high. The main US share index, the S&P 500, fell 0.25% that day. Over all of September it lost 0.5%.
levels.why: US rates affect savings, loans and exchange rates around the world.

levels.headline: The US central bank puts up interest rates
levels.body:
The US has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It sets the main interest rate in the US. That is the price of borrowing money. On 16 September it put the rate up a bit. It is now between 3.75% and 4%. It is the first rise since 2023, and everyone on the committee agreed.
The boss of the Fed is Kevin Warsh. He said that prices are still going up too fast. Investors think there will be at least one more rise this year, and more next year.
On 30 September there was some good news. US prices were rising slower than experts thought. But share prices still fell a little that day, and over the whole month.
levels.why: Higher US rates can make loans dearer in other countries too.

levels.headline: The US puts up interest rates to slow down rising prices
levels.body:
Every country has a bank that looks after its money. In the US, it is called the Federal Reserve, or the Fed. It sets an interest rate. That is the price of borrowing. On 16 September, the Fed made it go up for the first time since 2023. It is now between 3.75% and 4%.
Why? The Fed's boss, Kevin Warsh, said prices are still rising too fast. Raising rates makes borrowing cost more, and that can slow prices down. Experts think there will be at least one more rise this year.
On 30 September, new numbers showed prices rising a little more slowly than people thought. But the stock market fell a bit that day.
levels.why: It shows the US is working to slow down rising prices.

levels.why: US rates can change loan costs in other countries too.

levels.headline: The US bank raises its borrowing price to slow down prices
levels.body:
The US has a big bank for the whole country, called the Federal Reserve. It sets the price of borrowing money. We call this the interest rate. On 16 September, the bank made the price go up for the first time since 2023. It is now between 3.75% and 4%.
Why? Because things are getting more expensive. The boss of the bank, Kevin Warsh, said prices are still going up too fast. When borrowing costs more, people spend a bit less, and that helps prices to stop climbing so fast.
On 30 September there was a little good news. Prices were going up more slowly than people thought. But the stock market, where people buy and sell parts of companies, still fell a bit.
levels.why: It is a way to stop things getting too expensive.

levels.why: It is an effort to stop things getting too expensive.

levels.headline: The big bank in America has made borrowing cost more

America has a big bank for the whole country. It is called the Federal Reserve. It decides how much extra people pay when they borrow money. This extra is called interest.
On 16 September, the bank made the extra a little bigger. It is the first time since 2023. Now it is between 3.75p and 4p for every £1 borrowed for a year, if you count in pounds.
Why? Things in shops are getting dearer. The boss of the bank, Kevin Warsh, said prices are going up too fast. When borrowing costs more, people spend a bit less. That can help stop prices rising.

levels.why: It is a way to stop pocket money buying less and less.

headline: Eurozone inflation back above 3% on energy costs as September estimate looms

terms.meaning: The 21 EU countries that use the euro as their currency
The European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone
An early first estimate published before the full data is ready

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation back above 3% on energy costs as September estimate looms
levels.body:
Inflation across the euro area rose to 3.3% in August, according to Eurostat's flash estimate published on 1 September, up from 2.9% in July. Eurostat's later update on 17 September put the annual rate at 3.2%.
Energy prices are driving the rise. CNBC reported that the return above 3% made higher interest rates from the European Central Bank likely.
The next flash estimate, covering September, is due on 2 October. National figures released so far suggest the euro-area figure could exceed the ECB's baseline estimates, and strong European inflation data was one factor weighing on London and other European shares on 30 September.
The pressure mirrors what is happening in the UK, where inflation rose to 3.1% in August, and in the US, where the Federal Reserve raised rates this month.
levels.why: Rising inflation in the UK's biggest trading partner raises the chance of higher interest rates across Europe.

levels.headline: Euro area inflation at 3.2% to 3.3% as energy prices bite
levels.body:
Euro area inflation reached 3.3% in Eurostat's flash estimate for August, published on 1 September, up from 2.9% in July. A later release on 17 September showed 3.2%.
Higher energy prices are the main driver, and CNBC said the rise above 3% makes higher ECB interest rates likely.
The September flash estimate comes on 2 October. National data suggest that it could come in above the ECB's baseline. On 30 September, hot inflation data from Europe was one reason London shares gave up early gains.
The trend matches the UK, where CPI is 3.1%, and the US, where the Fed has just raised rates.
levels.why: Higher European rates would affect the pound and borrowing costs on both sides of the Channel.

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation above 3% again, driven by energy
levels.body:
Prices in the euro area were 3.3% higher in August than a year earlier, according to Eurostat's first estimate on 1 September. In July the figure was 2.9%. A later update on 17 September gave 3.2%.
Higher energy costs are the main cause. News reports said the rise makes higher interest rates from the European Central Bank likely.
The first estimate for September is due on 2 October. Figures from individual countries suggest it could be higher than the ECB expected. On 30 September, strong inflation numbers from Europe helped to pull London's shares lower.
The same pattern is seen in the UK and the US.
levels.why: Rising prices across Europe could lead to higher interest rates there.

levels.headline: Prices in the eurozone are rising faster again
levels.body:
The eurozone is the group of countries in Europe that use the euro. In August, prices there were 3.3% higher than a year before, according to a first estimate on 1 September. In July the rise was 2.9%. A later check on 17 September said 3.2%.
The main cause is the higher cost of energy. Reports said this makes higher interest rates from the European Central Bank, or ECB, likely.

headline: China's factories return to growth in September after two months of contraction

levels.headline: China's factories return to growth in September after two months of contraction
levels.body:
China's official manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index rose to 50.1 in September, up 0.3 points from August, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. A reading above 50 signals expansion, and the figure ended two months of contraction.
The production sub-index climbed 1.3 points to 51.7, while the new orders index stood at 50.5, still above the 50 threshold. Of the 21 industries surveyed, 12 reported a reading above 50, led by equipment manufacturing, high-tech manufacturing and consumer goods.
The data came after Beijing announced a stimulus package to offset economic strain and low consumer spending in the world's second-largest economy.
The improvement is modest, but it is a positive sign for China's leaders and for exporters worldwide, including the UK, that rely on Chinese demand and supply chains.
levels.why: China's factories influence global prices and trade, so a return to growth is good news for many economies.
